transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercado (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Patel (Veridian CTO), Liam O'Neal (Veridian Head of ML), Sara Kim (Veridian Security), Omar Ruiz (Product)

Summary:
Quick POC scoping focused on data handling for a Veridian Health pilot: PII/PHI concerns, logging/redaction, retention windows, prompt storage, and acceptable bench targets (qps & latency). Agreed to a 2-week Dedicated trial with a benchmark run; next steps defined.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone thanks for carving out time, uh this is Alex from Redwood, I'm the account lead. With me is Priya and Ethan from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Maya: Good thanks, thanks Alex. Ready to dig in.
[00:15] Liam: Yeah excited. We put security on the calendar because the PII questions are heavy here.
[00:20] Sara: Hi, Sara from security — we'll focus on where data lives, logs, and what gets persisted.

[00:30] Priya: Cool, quick agenda: we want to align on success criteria for the POC, workload sizing to size the trial, benchmarks to run, timelines, and then deep dive on data handling — redaction, retention, prompt storage. Sound okay?
[00:40] Omar: Yep. Important for us: HIPAA constraints and auditability.

[01:05] Priya: Great. Could you share current architecture? Liam?
[01:10] Liam: Sure. We're running inference in house for some beta features but it's expensive; majority of customer traffic hits our API, we proxy requests through an internal gateway, and logs are pushed to Splunk. For POC we'd like to offload the model serving to Redwood Dedicated if possible — must be able to keep traffic within our VPC and leverage our KMS keys.
[01:32] Priya: Ok, Redwood Dedicated supports VPC peering and private endpoints; we also support a Private deployment if you need the entire control plane inside your network. We can also integrate with customer-managed KMS for key rotation.
[01:45] Sara: Important: we cannot have full prompts stored in plain text longer than X days. We need redaction for PHI fields, and we need an option to entirely disable persistent logging of prompt text.
[02:02] Ethan: Understood. We have a few levers: retention windows (retention can be configured per-customer), query-level redaction at the edge, and an option to store only embeddings or hashed prompt metadata for telemetry. By default our hosted logs capture full prompts for 30 days for debugging, but for Dedicated/Private we can change that — or ship without storing raw prompt text.
[02:28] Maya: Can you confirm whether the KV cache or model checkpoints ever persist prompts?
[02:35] Priya: KV cache is in-memory per GPU node and is ephemeral for inference sessions — it's not written to disk unless you explicitly enable snapshotting. We can guarantee no persistent snapshots for the POC. However, a caveat: certain performance features like prefix caching could be configured to persist to disk for warm start; we would disable that for your pilot.
[03:00] Liam: Good. Performance caveat noted. For our success criteria we have three pillars: 1) latency: 95th percentile under 450ms for typical 256-token responses, 2) cost: less than our current $0.045 per 1k tokens average, and 3) correctness: acceptable F1 on our QA prompts > 0.85.
[03:25] Alex: Those are reasonable. For latency we usually run the benchmark with 50 concurrent users to simulate production; we can tweak concurrency. For cost we can show quantization suggestions and batching to get unit economics down.
[03:40] Priya: For the benchmark plan I'll propose three phases: baseline (single model, no batching), scaled concurrency (50-200 concurrent), and redaction-on-the-fly (measure CPU overhead for redaction + latency impact). We'll capture p95/p99, throughput (qps), and GPU utilization.
[03:58] Omar: How do you handle redaction? Is it pre-send (client-side) or server-side? We have some data that cannot leave client boundary.
[04:06] Ethan: We support both. Client-side redaction is the safest — you can mask PHI before it leaves your network. For server-side we provide a redact middleware that tokenizes and removes known PHI fields using regex and a configurable PII detector. That middleware can run on the edge inside your VPC if using Private/Dedicated.
[04:28] Sara: If we use server-side redaction we need audit logs showing which fields were redacted and why, with hashes of original values for traceability (not the original text). Is that supported?
[04:38] Priya: We can support hashed fingerprints in audit logs — we store salted hashes for traceability and we can surface allowlist/blocklist events. Those logs are put into your Splunk via our secure syslog connector or S3 sinks depending on your ingestion preference.
[04:55] Maya: What about prompt storage for evals — we run human-in-the-loop reviews and need to persist some prompts for labeling, but those prompts may contain PHI; can we configure a narrower retention specifically for audit/eval?
[05:10] Alex: Yes we can. For POC we recommend a short retention window (e.g., 7 days) for raw prompts, plus an opt-in secure eval export where we can mask PHI and only surface labeled fields. The eval export can be pushed to an S3 bucket you control and encrypted with your KMS.
[05:28] Liam: For benchmarking, we will share a redacted sample dataset (10k prompts) but we also want to test edge cases with full PHI — we need a secure way to do that for internal-only runs.
[05:40] Ethan: For those runs we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with a VPC peering and no internet egress. You can load full data via a secure bastion or our SFTP ingestion in your VPC. We'll also sign an NDA if needed.
[05:55] Sara: Are there any logs that leak partial prompt tokens into monitoring systems, like traces or span tags? We run automated audits for sensitive data.
[06:04] Priya: Good question. Default tracing includes operation IDs and token counts, but not raw tokens. If you enable debug tracing we do capture snippets for debugging — for the POC we will not enable debug tracing. We can also filter spans before they leave the node.
[06:20] Maya: Can you store everything in our region? Data residency is important.
[06:24] Alex: Yes, Dedicated clusters can be provisioned in your chosen cloud region and the data paths stay within that region. Private deployments give even more control.
[06:35] Liam: On the benchmarks: regen behavior and temperature will impact token counts — we need reproducible runs. How do you recommend we lock configs?
[06:42] Priya: We'll version the model + config used and snapshot the request/response meta (not raw prompts unless you opt in). For reproducible runs we can use non-deterministic seeds off; we can also run a fixed-seed mode for evaluation.
[06:58] Omar: For the cost targets, do you provide pre-flight model quantization or smaller-variant suggestions automatically?
[07:04] Ethan: Redwood Optimize will analyze workloads and recommend quantization profiles and alternate model variants. For the POC we'll run the initial baseline on FP16 and a quantized int8 path to measure delta.
[07:18] Alex: Let's nail timeline. We propose: customer provides sample dataset & success criteria by 2026-03-22; Redwood shares security pack by 2026-03-20; we provision Dedicated trial cluster on 2026-03-29 and run benchmarks week of 2026-03-30. Follow-up to review results 2026-04-07. Does that work?
[07:37] Maya: That works if you can ensure redaction and retention controls are in place before cluster goes live.
[07:43] Priya: We'll disable persistent prompt logging by default for your cluster and enable the hashed-audit approach. We'll also provide a config doc showing toggles.
[07:52] Sara: We'll need SAML metadata to integrate SSO — Alex, can you send that?
[07:56] Alex: Yes I'll include SSO/SAML notes in the security pack.
[08:05] Liam: Bench specifics: our target is 200 qps steady-state with p95 < 450ms for 256-token responses. Can Redwood simulate spike traffic?
[08:15] Priya: Yes we can stress up to 500 qps for scaled tests; we'll instrument with JMeter or Locust and share scripts.
[08:24] Omar: Any caveats about KV cache eviction during bench? If you warm caches on one node can that skew p95 when traffic shifts?
[08:30] Ethan: We'll control cache behavior and run both cold and warm benchmarks to capture variance. For POC we'll run a warm-up phase to emulate production.
[08:40] Maya: For regulatory/compliance, can you provide evidence of encryption-in-transit & at-rest and key rotation proofs?
[08:46] Alex: Yes that's in the SOC2 pack; we'll include KMS rotation logs and architecture diagrams.
[08:52] Sara: One more — we need to avoid storing original prompts in backups or snapshots.
[08:56] Priya: Confirmed: no snapshots with raw prompts, and backup policies will exclude prompt payloads.
[09:05] Liam: Great. For the POC success criteria recap: p95 < 450ms at 200 qps, cost under target (we'll compare token economics post-bench), and F1 > 0.85 on QA prompts. Also sign-off on data handling & retention configuration.
[09:25] Alex: I'll capture those as acceptance criteria and include them in the pilot SOW.
[09:32] Omar: On the sample data — we'll provide a mapping of PII fields and expected redaction regexes.
[09:38] Ethan: We'll ingest that into our redact middleware config; we'll confirm false positives/negatives in the redaction test run.
[09:45] Maya: How long does it take to spin up a Dedicated trial cluster?
[09:48] Priya: Typically 3–5 business days once we have network/VPC details and a contact for AWS/GCP role setup. For Private it's longer. For your timeline a 2026-03-29 start is achievable.
[09:59] Sara: Any live demo of the redaction UI?
[10:02] Priya: We can demo it in the next meeting; it's a small UI that shows redaction hits and audit hashes. We'll include screenshots in the security pack.
[10:10] Alex: Ok to wrap — recap next steps and owners.
[10:14] Maya: Sounds good.
[10:17] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the security pack and benchmark plan.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlaps, some product names mildly misspelled (e.g., Redwood Optimize sometimes heard as "Redwood Opti-mize"), occasional filler words removed.
